attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay. He is paraphrasing Altman's roadmap, but the paraphrase and its framing are his.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'it would appear' hedge, and the drafter set the modality to 'likely'. This is an epistemically hedged reading of Altman's post, with rhetorical overstatement ('won't be a model at all', 'rat king', 'mediocre').

contract.note: The contract scores a hedged statement on a plain reading, which policy limits to firm language. It also rescues the literal wording: it recasts 'won't be a model at all' as system integration and 'no longer letting you use' as standalone access. The speaker did not supply those readings.

evidence.note: Altman's dated roadmap post. It says GPT-5 will be a system integrating o3 and that o3 will not ship standalone. That matches the factual core of the paraphrase, not the 'mediocre' judgment.
Same-day TechCrunch report confirming that the standalone o3 launch was dropped in favour of integrating it into GPT-5.

reviews.rationale: The evidence confirms the core of the paraphrase: GPT-5 was to be an integrated system including o3, and o3 would not ship standalone. But Zitron framed it as a hedged reading ('it would appear') wrapped in rhetoric. Hedged language is not scored under policy, and a literal reading of 'won't be a model at all' and losing all access to o3 overstates the roadmap. Not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own unhedged assertion in his essay.

semantics.note: Taking the year as 2024 from the surrounding 'last year' discussion is reasonable. 'Approximately' and 'compute alone' are preserved.

contract.note: Treating 'approximately $5B' as $4.5–5.5B is an ordinary plain reading. The contract rightly requires a reconciled full-year figure and asks that cash spending and recognised expense be kept apart.

evidence.note: Epoch's ~$7B estimate of 2024 cloud compute falls outside the range. But it rests partly on Q4 projections and an assumed amortisation schedule, so it is not reliable enough to beat the accounting uncertainty.

reviews.rationale: The only accessible estimate (Epoch, ~$7B) is above the claimed figure. It relies on projections and assumed amortisation, and the packet says no verified full-year reconciliation of compute costs was found. The evidence neither confirms ~$5B nor contradicts it with the precision the contract requires.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, building on the 11M subscriber figure he cites in the same passage.

semantics.note: The hypothetical 300M MAU denominator is preserved, 'piss-poor' is kept as opinion, and the revenue-majority premise is kept.

contract.note: The arithmetic test is fair. The speaker gave no revenue period, so using realized calendar-2024 revenue is the evaluator's choice. It is an ordinary reading, though the present-tense 'makes up' could also fit a point-in-time revenue mix.

evidence.note: WSJ (Oct 2024) reports 11M paying subscribers. 11M ÷ 300M ≈ 3.67%, which is below 4%.
The CFO says about 75% of revenue comes from consumer subscriptions, but names no completed accounting period. It is a company disclosure. Its 5–6% conversion figure uses a different denominator.

reviews.rationale: The arithmetic holds: 11M ÷ 300M ≈ 3.7%, under 4%. The revenue premise is backed only by a CFO remark from Oct 2024 with no stated period, and the packet found no realized 2024 revenue mix. The contract requires both parts for support, so the claim as a whole is not settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own description of reasoning models in his essay.

semantics.note: This is a compound claim. It keeps 'mostly', 'a bit more accurate', the mechanism (more tokens, multiple models checking), and the speed/cost tradeoff. The 'one big thing' and consciousness parts can't be tested.

contract.note: Testing each component separately is fair. Reading 'a bit more accurate' as a modest gain is the plain reading. The contract rightly says 'mostly' cannot be settled without a representative task distribution.

evidence.note: OpenAI concedes that models like o1 can be expensive and slow, which backs the cost/speed part. It is a company disclosure.
OpenAI's own evaluations show large gains on reasoning benchmarks (AIME ~12% to 74%), not 'a bit' more accurate. These are self-reported and limited to selected tasks.
DeepSeek's paper describes self-verification inside one model's long chain of thought. That contradicts multiple models checking each other as the mechanism, while backing the extra-tokens part.
Compares one reasoning model with another (o3-mini vs o1-mini), so it does not test reasoning against non-reasoning models.

reviews.rationale: These parts hold: reasoning uses more tokens and costs more in money and speed (e1, e3). These are contradicted by dated documentation: that 'multiple models check the work' (e3 shows checking inside one model), and that gains are only modest on documented reasoning benchmarks (e2, self-reported). 'Mostly', 'one big thing' and consciousness remain unsettled or untestable.
